name: Citation Graphs Over Time
title: Citation Graphs Over Time
answer: Citation graphs over time model scholarly literature as a network where papers are nodes and citations are directed edges, then track how that network changes across years. The scope includes the growth of the graph, the rise and fall of individual papers, shifts in which venues and authors are central, and the movement of ideas between fields. It also covers the temporal patterns of citation, such as how quickly a paper accumulates citations and how long it continues to be cited. Researchers use these graphs to study influence, discovery, and the structure of scientific communities.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Citation graphs over time model scholarly literature as a network where papers are nodes and citations are directed edges, then track how that network changes across years. The scope includes the growth of the graph, the rise and fall of individual papers, shifts in which venues and authors are central, and the movement of ideas between fields. It also covers the temporal patterns of citation, such as how quickly a paper accumulates citations and how long it continues to be cited. Researchers use these graphs to study influence, discovery, and the structure of scientific communities.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on large bibliographic databases and citation indexes that provide metadata for papers, authors, venues, and references. Common sources include Crossref, OpenAlex, and Semantic Scholar, which offer APIs and bulk data for building graphs. Storage and computation often use graph databases or columnar data stores, with processing frameworks that can handle billions of edges. Because the data is large and changes over time, pipelines typically take regular snapshots and maintain versioned copies.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Building a citation graph over time starts with extracting references from papers, resolving them to unique identifiers such as DOIs, and linking them to the cited works. Researchers then construct a series of time stamped graphs, one for each year or month, and compute network measures like in degree, PageRank, and betweenness centrality on each snapshot. They also apply community detection to see how clusters of papers form and split, and use burst detection to find sudden increases in citations. For prediction tasks, they may train models on past graph states to forecast future citations or emerging topics.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in citation graphs center on the provenance and licensing of the underlying metadata and full text. Citation data from commercial indexes may have terms of use that restrict redistribution, while open sources like Crossref and OpenAlex have their own licenses. Risks include coverage bias, where some regions, languages, or disciplines are underrepresented, and citation manipulation, where authors or journals artificially inflate counts. Good practice is to record the source and version of every edge, to respect retractions and corrections, and to link to the original paper rather than a third party summary.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward finer temporal resolution, with graphs updated continuously rather than yearly, and toward richer nodes that include datasets, software, and preprints. Dynamic graph neural networks and temporal link prediction are becoming standard for modeling how citations evolve. There is also growing interest in open citation data and in tools that let researchers explore the time dimension interactively. As more of the scholarly record becomes machine readable, citation graphs over time will increasingly support discovery, evaluation, and the study of science itself.
